Definition & Facts of Urinary Retention - NIDDK

content.text:
Not being able to empty your bladder completely is called **urinary retention**. It can happen for two big reasons: **something is blocking urine flow**, or **the bladder muscle/nerves aren’t working well enough to push urine out**. ([niddk.nih.gov](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/urinary-retention/symptoms-causes?utm_source=openai))

Common causes include:

- **Enlarged prostate** in men, which can squeeze the urethra and slow/stop urine flow.
- **Urinary tract infection (UTI)** or inflammation, which can cause swelling and make it hard to pee.
- **Constipation**, which can press on the bladder or urethra.
- **Certain medications**, especially some antihistamines, decongestants, antidepressants, sedatives, muscle relaxers, and some bladder-control medicines.
- **Nerve problems** from diabetes, stroke, multiple sclerosis, spinal cord problems/injury, or pelvic surgery.
- **Weak bladder muscle** or “underactive bladder,” where the bladder can’t contract strongly enough.
- **Urethral narrowing/stricture**, scar tissue, bladder stones, or tumors.
- **Pelvic organ prolapse** in women, where pelvic organs drop and interfere with bladder emptying.
- **Recent surgery/anesthesia**, which can temporarily cause retention.

**Get urgent medical care now** if you **cannot urinate at all**, have severe lower belly pain/swelling, fever, vomiting, new back/flank pain, weakness/numbness in the legs, or blood in the urine. Acute urinary retention can be serious and may need a catheter to drain the bladder. ([niddk.nih.gov](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/urinary-retention/definition-facts?utm_source=openai))

If this is ongoing but you can still urinate, it’s still worth seeing a clinician/urologist. They may check a urine test, kidney function, prostate/pelvic exam, and a bladder scan after you pee to see how much urine is left.
